conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, anxiety, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team.

I’ll read each question conversationally—just tell me what feels true for you. If any question feels hard, we can pause or reword it. Ready to start?

1. Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Hi, Sarah… sure, we can go ahead.

Um, I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes, but I guess it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Like, if my partner makes a joke I’ll still chuckle, but it feels kind of forced and I don’t really feel it inside. So, overall, I’d say “yes, but not as much as before.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes yes, but definitely not as much as I used to. I can still laugh if something’s really funny, but it feels kind of flat—like I’m going through the motions more than actually feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really, if I’m honest. I used to get excited about little plans—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just a walk—but lately it feels like, “what’s the point?” I still do them, but more because I think I should, not because I’m looking forward to them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby won’t settle, I’ll think maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. Most of the time I know it’s not actually my fault, but those “what did I do wrong?” thoughts still pop in a few times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I’d say yes, pretty often. Most of it’s about the baby—like, I’ll lie awake wondering if his breathing sounds normal or if he’s gaining enough weight, even when the pediatrician just said he’s fine. I know in my head there’s no real reason to worry, but I still feel tense and on-edge a lot of the day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but there are moments—especially at night—when my heart starts racing and I feel kind of shaky. It’s like a sudden wave of “something bad could happen to the baby” even though everything looks fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m barely keeping my head above water. Between the feedings, the pumping, trying to sleep in tiny windows, and just keeping the baby safe, it piles up. I’m not falling apart, but I do end the day exhausted and thinking, “I don’t know how I’ll do this all again tomorrow.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say it’s exactly “unhappy” keeping me awake—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie down after the baby finally sleeps, and suddenly I’m replaying every little thing: did I swaddle him tight enough, is that sniffle something more, when will he wake again. It takes me a long time to drift off, and any little sound jolts me awake again.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—maybe every couple of days it hits me. It’s not this constant dark cloud, but I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. The feeling usually passes after an hour or so, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—mostly when I’m overly tired—but I haven’t actually cried in the past week. I get that heavy, about-to-cry feeling, but I manage to hold it back.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the last week has felt heavy: laughter arrives flat, plans feel pointless, and waves of worry about your baby sweep through the night. Even though you're doing everything 'right', you end most days exhausted and wondering how you'll manage tomorrow. These feelings are common in new motherhood, and you deserve support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports reduced ability to laugh and describes emotional blunting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no anticipatory pleasure and参与活动 purely out of obligation, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>She reports self-blaming thoughts several times daily, consistent with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, excessive worry about baby's health despite reassurance, feeling tense/on-edge most days, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, unexpected surges of fear/anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart, shakiness) that resolve quickly, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and exhaustion, indicating she is "barely keeping my head above water" and uncertain about tomorrow, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring: 17/30, well above the ≥14 threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core criteria met: <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> most days (Q1=2, Q2=3), <sym>fatigue</sym> and feeling overwhelmed (Q6=2), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> linked to ruminative worry (Q7=1), <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym> (Q3=2), and persistent <sym>anxiety</sym> with autonomic symptoms (Q4=3, Q5=2). No <med>self-harm ideation</med> (Q10=0). Pattern fits <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> specifiers: symptom onset within 4 weeks postpartum, anxious distress, moderate severity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss <med>antidepressant</med> and/or <med>CBT</med> options safe for breastfeeding
3. Encourage 15-min daytime rest periods; split night duties with support person when possible
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing at night to reduce <sym>nocturnal panic</sym>
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to track progress
6. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers for immediate support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview

Symptoms endorsed  
• Diminished pleasure/interest (laughing “flat,” activities feel pointless)  
• Irrational self-blame around infant care  
• Persistent, intrusive anxious worry re infant safety ➔ occasional nocturnal autonomic surge (racing heart, shakiness)  
• Sleep initiation/maintenance disturbance linked to ruminative worry  
• Intermittent tearfulness/sad mood, 2–3×/wk, self-limited, no frank crying spells  
• Subjective sense of “barely keeping head above water” most days

Areas of screening significance  
Mood: mild–moderate anhedonia, situational sadness  
Anxiety: generalized & situational (infant-focused), sub-panic episodes  
Coping: perceived daily overload, no self-harm ideation

Risk factors documented  
✓ Loss of enjoyment, intermittent dysphoria  
✓ Sleep disruption tied to mood state  
✓ Excessive guilt / self-criticism  
✓ Chronic heightened anxiety with nocturnal spikes  
✗ No self-harm or suicidal thoughts reported

Screening observation  
Responses indicate clinically significant symptoms consistent with postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; patient denies self-harm. Recommend formal assessment (EPDS scoring, clinical interview) to determine severity and intervention needs.
